summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles is resolved: the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct. Those articles reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy.

Enforcement against same-sex couples has historically run through public-order offences rather than a sodomy statute. A former law criminalising acts that violated "decorum and good behaviour" in public was used by police to harass, fine or jail same-sex couples for displays of affection; it was repealed by a 1997 amendment to the Criminal Code. In 2006 several gay clubs and bars in Santo Domingo were shut down as part of a police harassment programme, and in 2012 police broke up the Santo Domingo LGBT Pride Parade and arrested marchers on the ground that they were improperly using the national flag. Reports indicate that visible, politically active LGBTQ community signs are frequent targets of government crackdowns, sometimes with the support of religious leaders.

Transgender people cannot change their legal gender. A narrow route to changing legal name exists: in June 2018 President Danilo Medina issued an executive decree granting 35 transgender Dominicans the possibility of changing their legal name to match their gender identity, and television journalist Mía Cepeda was among the 35. A 2017 ILGA poll found that only 5% of Dominicans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

Family law statutes recognise no legal status between same-sex persons, neither marriage nor marriage-like relationships. The 2010 constitutional amendment added Article 55, under which the State shall promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, so same-sex marriage is constitutionally barred; households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the rights given to opposite-sex married couples. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on Private International Law could justify recognition of a foreign marriage, since a marriage is valid if considered such by the law of the place of celebration, national law or the domicile of at least one spouse. On 9 January 2018 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an advisory opinion that parties to the American Convention should grant same-sex couples access to all existing domestic family registration systems including marriage, and several Dominican legal experts have said the country must implement it.

Discrimination on account of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal in health care, employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services or public accommodations, and many LGBTQ people consequently remain in the closet. The exception is Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS, which since 2011 has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review left in place the absence of a general anti-discrimination statute and of marriage recognition.

The prevailing climate is shaped by the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant denominations, whose socially conservative mores hold significant sway over public policy and attitudes. Because most residents hold conservative views, the major political parties have not expressed much public support for LGBTQ rights legislation. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 69% of Dominicans said people in same-sex relationships should be charged as criminals, a finding that sits alongside the absence of any criminal prohibition and indicates the risk of hostility rather than of prosecution.
tangentialFactors:
The backlash against openly gay U.S. Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster, who presented with his husband in Santo Domingo in June 2015, is the clearest documented instance of organised domestic opposition: attacks followed on LGBT Dominicans, religious leaders and some politicians regularly insulted him, and evangelical groups ran an unsuccessful petition asking the government to expel him, telling him to "go home and cook since he's married to a man." His departure in 2017 after two years of visible presence, including speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016, left an advocacy void and exposed a polarised climate.

Counterweights exist. The Dominican Republic has accepted recommendations at its Universal Periodic Review on the rights of intersex persons and on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, an international-commitment record for which the sources show no domestic implementation detail. In April 2017 more than 300 activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo at which Dominican government officials spoke. Organised trans advocacy has deep roots: COTRAVETD, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, was co-founded in 2004 and is led by executive director Nairovi Castillo, whose first-hand account of trans struggles in the country was published on Transgender Day of Visibility in 2019.

Regional comparators matter here. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018 binds parties to the American Convention in the direction of recognising same-sex couples, and Dominican legal experts have asserted an obligation to implement it, though the sources record no implementing legislation. The country's own record on HIV-related discrimination, through Law 135/2011, is more protective than its general equality framework, a pattern common in the region.
localsOnly:
Transgender Dominicans have no statutory right to change legal gender; the June 2018 executive decree under President Danilo Medina addressed legal name only and benefited 35 named individuals, television journalist Mía Cepeda among them. Public opinion measured in 2017 placed support for legal gender change at 5%.

Residents have a constitutional right to access health care services, but health care programmes serving the LGBTQ community have generally focused on HIV/AIDS education and are often run by non-governmental organisations such as Amigos Siempre Amigos. Law 135/2011 on HIV/AIDS has since 2011 prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity; no general anti-discrimination statute covers employment, education, housing, banking, transportation, government services or public accommodations.

Same-sex couples hold no recognised legal status. Article 55 of the constitution, added by the 2010 amendment, directs the State to promote and protect family organisation based on marriage between a man and a woman, and households headed by same-sex couples receive none of the rights attached to opposite-sex marriage. Article 41 of Law 544-14 on Private International Law leaves open recognition of a marriage celebrated abroad where the law of the place of celebration, national law or the domicile of one spouse treats it as valid, and several Dominican legal experts hold that the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion must be implemented; no implementing measure is recorded in the sources.

The political parties have not publicly championed LGBTQ rights legislation against the weight of Catholic and evangelical conservative opinion, which a 2017 ILGA poll measured at 69% favouring criminal charges for people in same-sex relationships. Community organisations such as COTRAVETD, co-founded in 2004, and NGOs including Amigos Siempre Amigos carry much of the service and advocacy work.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not address how Dominican border and immigration authorities treat transgender visitors whose passports or entry documents do not match their presentation, nor whether any screening at entry could expose a traveller's gender identity. Nothing is sourced on the treatment of foreign identity documents generally.

Unresolved: the enforcement scope of Law 135/2011 beyond the HIV context is not detailed in the inventory, including whether its non-discrimination protection is used in practice or what penalties attach. The UPR database records accepted recommendations on intersex rights and on sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination without showing any domestic implementing measure; whether such measures exist is not sourced here.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory states whether hate-crime or hate-speech provisions cover anti-LGBTQ motivation, and no post-2024 data is available on police conduct toward LGBTQ people following the Constitutional Court's review. The claim that several Dominican legal experts consider the Inter-American Court's 2018 advisory opinion binding is recorded without naming those experts or any court ruling applying it.
